entities.name: Ghaznavids
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Ghaznavid dynasty was a Turkic Muslim dynasty that ruled from Ghazni (in modern Afghanistan) from 977 to 1186 CE, renowned for creating one of the Islamic world's most culturally brilliant courts and for the military campaigns of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni (r. 998-1030 CE) that brought Islam to the Indian subcontinent through 17 devastating raids on northern India. The Ghaznavids created a Persian-language court culture that patronized poets including Firdausi (author of the Shahnameh) and al-Biruni, who accompanied Mahmud to India and wrote the first systematic account of Indian geography and religion.

Mahmud of Ghazni's 17 raids into India (1001-1027 CE) were primarily motivated by treasure, not permanent conquest: he looted Hindu temples including Somnath (1025), destroying what Muslims considered idols and Muslims as the iconoclasm of victorious faith, taking enormous wealth back to beautify Ghazni. These raids established patterns of Islamic-Hindu conflict that persist in historical memory to this day.

Al-Biruni's accompanying Mahmud to India produced Kitab al-Hind (Book of India, 1030), the most comprehensive account of Indian science, mathematics, philosophy, and religion written in the medieval Islamic world. The Ghaznavid dynasty was eventually displaced by the Ghurids; their cultural legacy persisted through the Persianate court culture that shaped all subsequent Islamic dynasties in South Asia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Ghaznavids' 17 Indian raids established the earliest pattern of Islamic-Hindu military conflict still contested in South Asian historical memory, while their Persian court culture shaped Islamic civilization from Central Asia to India for centuries.
